teaser: A proposal: every agent takes a behaviour policy beside its prompt, which the vendor accepts and answers for, as aviation and payments learned to.
core_idea: Beside the system prompt and the prompt, every agent should take an Agent Behaviour Policy written to a published standard, which the vendor acknowledges row by row, enforces where it can, reports breaches against and eventually answers for, because agent behaviour is becoming an existential risk to the vendors through liability and trust, and aviation and payments show that safety follows when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way.

nodes.label: A third input
nodes.summary: A behaviour policy beside the system prompt and the prompt, versioned and loaded by the platform.

nodes.label: Code and data in one channel
nodes.summary: Models do not separate instructions from content, so prompt injection may never be fully fixed.

nodes.label: A second channel
nodes.summary: The policy takes the instructions that matter most out of the channel anyone can write into.

nodes.label: An existential risk
nodes.summary: Liability and above all trust: a few people badly hurt can make many stop giving agents instructions.

nodes.label: Aviation
nodes.summary: At 1995's rate, 2025's flights would have brought about 105 fatal airliner accidents; there were 12.

nodes.label: Payments
nodes.summary: Liability moved onto card companies and banks, and the security and detection followed the loss.

nodes.label: Fines are not enough
nodes.summary: Some industries pay the fines; improvement comes when rule, liability and business model align.

nodes.label: Inside and outside the policy
nodes.summary: The vendor answers for the rows it accepted; the user for everything the policy does not cover.

nodes.label: A competitive advantage
nodes.summary: A vendor that keeps more rows as boundaries can sell that as the product.

nodes.label: What the standard needs
nodes.summary: A versioned policy file, per-row acknowledgement, the vendor's own policy, breach reports, liability per row.

nodes.label: Hidden vendor policies
nodes.summary: Claude in Chrome will not type a password: a policy we cannot see, rely on, or stop changing.

nodes.label: Reverse-engineer them
nodes.summary: Measure the policies agents already run and publish them in the ABP format.

nodes.label: Both modes are hope today
nodes.summary: Over the API the policy goes in our system prompt; in the Claude apps and Claude Code after the vendor's; either way the model is asked to keep it.

nodes.label: A system prompt is a light policy
nodes.summary: It tells the agent how to behave; it should be written as rows, layered: the vendor's policy, then the deployer's.

quotes.text: The moment you pass the liability for fraud to the company, its security picks up.
quotes.why: The payments lesson the proposal rests on.

quotes.text: So the user enters the password, because Claude says, I am not going to put a password in.
quotes.why: A vendor policy already running, invisible and unguaranteed.

figures.caption: What an agent is given, today in two modes and as proposed. Over the API we write the whole system prompt, so our behaviour policy goes inside it; in the Claude apps and Claude Code the vendor's system prompt comes first and our policy goes into what we add. In both, it is text the model is asked to keep, in the same channel as every email and page it reads, and the vendor's checks are its own. Proposed: the policy as a separate, versioned input, layered over the vendor's own published policy, checked outside the model where it can be.

Fatal airliner accidents, 1995 and 2025. At 1995's rate of 2.72 per million flights, 2025's 38.7 million flights would have produced about 105 fatal accidents. There were 12. Rates from the Aviation Safety Network via Our World in Data; 2025 accidents from the Flight Safety Foundation's report of the ASN data; flights from IATA.

Where the liability for payment fraud was moved, and what followed. Each step put the loss on the party best placed to stop it, and the security followed the loss: caps for consumers, a liability shift onto whoever had not adopted chip cards, standards written by the card brands, and reimbursement of scam victims.

The proposed split. The vendor publishes its own built-in policy and accepts the deployer's; for every row it accepts, it says what enforces it and answers if it breaks. Everything the policy does not cover stays with the user, as it does today. The vendors that keep more rows as boundaries can sell that as the product.
